Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
avoid anything that could be stressful
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are strongly social-evaluative and interpersonal (avoiding evaluation, avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which contains no social threat, shame, or interpersonal trauma content to explain these strategies.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, the strongest pathway is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies. However, the selected negative appraisals focus on global identity change, chronic misery, and self-blame for being in the situation, while the selected strategies are specifically about managing social scrutiny and interpersonal interactions. That is a weak clinical fit: the strategies do not plausibly follow from the appraisals provided.

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Memory and appraisals are only partly coherent: terror on recall and olfactory recall fit disaster trauma, but rage on recall is less well supported by the rest of the profile because there is no accompanying appraisal about betrayal, preventability by others, or injustice that would explain intense anger as a central recall response.

For a natural-disaster trauma, intense rage specifically on recall is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on terror, misery, self-change, and generalized avoidance rather than anger at a person or agent. Rage can occur, but here it lacks support from the other selected items and is the least coherent memory item.

'Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation' implies preventable personal failure in getting into the trauma. With a natural disaster, this appraisal is difficult to justify unless there was a very specific risky decision context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other appraisals focus on post-trauma change and unhappiness, making this item the clearest mismatch.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, strong self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to justify clinically unless the disaster involved a very specific preventable action by the patient. In the absence of any such context, this appraisal is implausible for the indexed trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are predominantly interpersonal/social-safety behaviors (avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations) that fit social threat or shame-based trauma formulations more than a natural disaster PTSD presentation. They do not connect well to the memory/appraisal content provided.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile includes active hypervigilant threat-monitoring ('constantly scan environment for signs of threat') and a global danger appraisal, but the formulation specifies Threat as effectively inactive, with no active links involving Threat and no active Trigger pathways. For a natural-disaster case, these items imply an ongoing threat-focused maintenance pattern that is not supported by the stated formulation.

issues.item: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
issues.explanation: This is not just a weak-edge issue: both items explicitly center current external danger/threat, whereas the active formulation is concentrated on Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory and Negative Appraisals ↔ Maladaptive Strategies without Threat involvement. The remaining items fit a self-focused/post-traumatic change formulation, making these threat-focused items the main incoherent elements.

vignette:
Caleb, a 19-year-old single man of North American background, works the morning shift at a fast food restaurant in a mid-sized Midwestern town. He was referred for psychological assessment following a brief conversation with his shift supervisor, who had noticed a marked change in his demeanour over the preceding months. Caleb arrived at the intake session quiet and visibly tense, choosing his words with unusual care - pausing before each answer as though rehearsing it first.

Approximately eight months prior to the intake, Caleb had been at home alone when a severe tornado struck his neighbourhood without adequate warning. He had no time to reach a shelter. He described pressing himself into the corner of a bathroom as the roof above him partially gave way, the air pressure dropping sickeningly, the smell of wet earth and splintered wood filling the space around him. The sound was what he remembered most viscerally - a roaring that he said felt alive, like something was trying to swallow the house whole. He stayed there for what he later learned was eleven minutes but experienced as something without duration. When it was over, the neighbourhood was largely unrecognisable. He walked out into a street strewn with insulation and shattered glass, still in his socks.

In the weeks that followed, the memories returned not as coherent narratives but as fragments - predominantly images: the wall bowing inward, the light fixture swinging violently, the shadow of debris crossing the window. These visual memories arrived without warning and were accompanied by the same terror he had felt in the moment, a physiological flooding that left him shaking and breathless. On several occasions, particularly during outdoor shifts when the wind picked up or when a customer left the restaurant door open and the smell of rain drifted in, the olfactory memory returned with startling precision - wet earth and wood - and Caleb would find himself momentarily back inside that bathroom. The intrusive quality of these memories, their sensory immediacy and the terror they carried, began to convince him that something fundamental had broken inside him. He had come to believe that the person he had been before the tornado - easy-going, sociable, someone his coworkers had described as reliably cheerful - was simply gone, replaced by someone he did not recognise and did not like.

These appraisals of permanent, irreversible change shaped the strategies Caleb began building around himself. Certain that he was damaged in ways that could not be repaired, and that any additional stress might confirm or deepen that damage, he began systematically avoiding anything that felt even mildly threatening. At work, this meant he stopped volunteering for tasks that required him to go outside to collect trolleys or take out bins - situations where weather was unpredictable. He also began rehearsing conversations before approaching a manager or answering a customer complaint, terrified that he would say the wrong thing or appear visibly distressed. He tried hard not to think about the tornado at all, suppressing the memories whenever they surfaced, which had the effect of keeping him in a state of constant low-level vigilance, braced against the next intrusion.

The suppression did not work. The memories returned with the same intensity, and each time they did, the terror they carried felt like fresh evidence that he was right - that the damage was real and permanent. The more the memories confirmed his worst fears about himself, the more rigidly he applied his avoidance strategies; and the more he avoided, the more his world contracted, and the more miserable and unrecognisable he became to himself. His social life had effectively ceased. He had stopped responding to messages from friends he had known since high school. His mother had commented that he seemed like a different person. He agreed with her, privately, and found no comfort in the agreement.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a shift at work during which a sudden thunderstorm sent him into the walk-in freezer to avoid the sound of the rain on the metal roof - and a coworker found him there, standing alone in the cold, unable to explain himself. He was ashamed, but more than that, he was frightened. What he most feared, he said quietly at the end of the intake session, was that this was simply who he was now. What he most hoped was that someone could tell him otherwise.
